title: Bài sưu tầm 223 - Passage 2: Listening to Glaciers: The Acoustics of Melting Ice
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 223

Listening to Glaciers: The Acoustics of Melting Ice

Paragraph A. High above the polar ice sheets, Earth-observing cameras look down from orbit, tracking where white ice edges retreat year after year. Yet those overhead images reveal little about what happens out of sight—at the freezing boundary where millions of tonnes of ice slide across bedrock or melt inside dark undersea cavities. Drilling boreholes straight down through kilometres of shifting ice is slow, costly, and risky for equipment. To peer beneath the frozen crust without breaking it, glaciologists are increasingly swapping drills for acoustic sensors, turning passive sound recording into a window on ice collapse.

Paragraph B. To the untrained ear, a polar fjord sounds deceptively tranquil, broken only by the occasional thunder of an iceberg snapping off a cliff. In reality, glacier fronts are among the noisiest natural underwater environments on the planet. As falling snow compresses into glacial ice over centuries, tiny pockets of ancient air become trapped under immense weight. When warm ocean currents eat away at the submerged base of a glacier, those compressed bubbles burst violently into the sea, producing a steady, high-pitched sizzle louder than heavy rain on a metal roof. By measuring the volume of that crackling chorus, scientists can estimate underwater melting rates far more precisely than surface photos allow.

Paragraph C. Deeper inland, away from ocean waves, acoustic sensors pick up a very different soundscape: the low, rhythmic groaning of ice grinding across rock. Moving glaciers do not glide effortlessly; basal friction holds the bottom layer back until built-up tension triggers sudden micro-quakes that jolt the ice forward a few centimetres at a time. In summer, when surface meltwater drains down vertical shafts to the glacier floor, it acts like a lubricant, reducing resistance and causing the deep rumbling signals to spike sharply. Tracking these seismic hums tells researchers almost immediately when a glacier begins accelerating toward the sea.

Paragraph D. In western Greenland, glaciologist Dr. Sofia Lindberg spent four winters deploying a network of acoustic listening posts along the Sermeq Kujalleq fjord. Rather than anchoring delicate recorders directly beside tumbling ice cliffs—where falling blocks routinely crush instruments—her team moored steel frames at a safe depth far below the reach of drifting icebergs. However, analysing the recordings posed an unexpected hurdle: harsh polar winds and cracking sea ice generated low-frequency background booms that closely resembled glacial movement, while thick winter sea ice prevented supply ships from reaching the sensors for eight months of the year to collect stored data.

Paragraph E. Listening beneath the waves has also revealed a surprising link between glacier noise and Arctic wildlife. In early spring, ringed seals and narwhals congregate just metres away from roaring underwater ice walls. Hydrophone arrays in Svalbard showed that rapidly melting tidewater fronts release plumes of freshwater that stir deep, nutrient-rich layers up to the surface, attracting dense swarms of krill and polar cod—making the noisy glacier face a vital seasonal feeding ground despite the deafening racket.

Paragraph F. Looking forward, polar engineers are pairing underwater microphones with automated satellite relays embedded inside drifting surface buoys, allowing melting alerts to reach climate laboratories within hours rather than years. Because remote orbital imaging alone can overlook hidden undersea erosion until an entire ice shelf suddenly gives way, listening to the hidden creaks and crackles of ice may provide coastal cities with crucial extra warning of future sea-level rise.

groups.title: Questions 14–19
groups.instructions:
Reading Passage 223 has six sections, A–F.
Which section contains the following information?
Write the correct letter, A–F, in boxes 14–19 on your answer sheet.

groups.title: Questions 20–21
groups.instructions:
Choose TWO letters, A–E.
Write the correct letters in boxes 20 and 21 on your answer sheet.

Which TWO findings or challenges from polar acoustic monitoring are mentioned in the passage?
options: A. Underwater recorders are too fragile to function in sub-zero ocean temperatures.
B. Frozen ocean surfaces can block researchers from retrieving data for much of the year.
C. Passing commercial cargo ships create more underwater noise than melting ice cliffs.
D. Rising plumes near noisy melting glaciers bring prey species closer to the surface for predators.
E. Acoustic sensors have completely replaced all orbital camera monitoring across Greenland.

groups.title: Questions 22–26
groups.instructions:
Complete the summary below.
Choose ONE WORD ONLY from the passage for each answer.
Write your answers in boxes 22–26 on your answer sheet.
groups.template:
Researchers measure underwater glacier melt by recording the sharp hissing produced when pressurised air 22. {{q22}} escape from dissolving ice. Further inland, sensors capture deep vibrations caused when stone and ice resist one another through basal 23. {{q23}} . During warmer months, this movement speeds up after surface 24. {{q24}} flows down to reduce resistance against the rock below.

To prevent passing icebergs from damaging delicate equipment, Dr. Sofia Lindberg secured her listening posts at a protected 25. {{q25}} on the seabed. Future stations will transmit findings quickly via 26. {{q26}} connections so scientists do not have to rely solely on overhead photographs.

q14.text: a reason why melting underwater glacier edges generate unexpectedly intense sound

steps: Đoạn B: Giải thích tuy nghe yên tĩnh nhưng chân sông băng dưới nước cực ồn do hàng triệu bọt khí nén lâu năm vỡ tung khi băng tan.

q15.text: an explanation of why marine mammals gather near loud glacial walls

steps: Đoạn E: Hải cẩu và kỳ lân biển tụ tập gần vách băng ồn ào vì dòng nước ngọt tan chảy đẩy dinh dưỡng lên thu hút nhuyễn thể và cá tuyết.

q16.text: limitations of existing visual and physical methods for studying hidden ice loss

steps: Đoạn A: Nêu hạn chế của camera vệ tinh (không thấy bên dưới) và khoan băng (chậm, tốn kém, dễ hỏng thiết bị).

q17.text: a future system designed to speed up the delivery of warning data to researchers

steps: Đoạn F: Kết hợp micro dưới nước với phao truyền tin vệ tinh tự động để gửi cảnh báo trong vài giờ thay vì chờ nhiều năm.

q18.text: an account of how seasonal warming alters the speed of ice sliding over land

steps: Đoạn C: Vào mùa hè nước tan từ bề mặt chảy xuống đáy đóng vai trò chất bôi trơn làm giảm ma sát, khiến sông băng trượt nhanh hơn.

q19.text: a practical way of positioning instruments to avoid physical collision with floating ice

steps: Đoạn D: Nhóm Lindberg neo khung thép ở độ sâu an toàn nằm dưới tầm va chạm của các tảng băng trôi.

Đoạn D: thick winter sea ice prevented supply ships from reaching the sensors for eight months of the year to collect stored data ↔ B (Băng biển mùa đông chặn tàu tiếp cận lấy dữ liệu trong phần lớn thời gian năm). (Bẫy: A sai vì hỏng là do băng rơi va đập chứ không phải do nhiệt độ lạnh; C không nhắc tàu thương mại; E sai vì chỉ bổ trợ chứ không thay thế hoàn toàn camera vệ tinh).
Đoạn E: plumes of freshwater that stir deep, nutrient-rich layers up to the surface, attracting dense swarms of krill and polar cod (thu hút hải cẩu và kỳ lân biển) ↔ D.
Đoạn C: stone and ice resist one another through basal friction.
Đoạn C: During warmer months = In summer; surface meltwater drains down.
Đoạn D: secured ... at a protected = moored steel frames at a safe depth.
